docs.title: django-spec-rest
docs.text:
Serve django-service-specs over Django REST Framework.

A kernel spec declares an operation once: the callable that runs it, the arguments it reads, who may call it, how its input is validated and how its result is presented. django-spec-rest serves that spec on a DRF view or viewset, and lets DRF fill three of its seats: a serializer validates the input (SerializerValidator), a serializer renders the result (SerializerPresenter), and DRF permission classes decide who may call it (DRFPermissionCheck). The same spec runs off HTTP through the kernel's own dispatch, and on any other transport that serves kernel specs.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Views and viewsets that take a kernel spec: ServiceCreateView, ServiceUpdateView, ServiceDeleteView, SelectorListView, SelectorRetrieveView, ServiceViewSet, SelectorViewSet, the per-action mixins, and @service_action / @selector_action for custom routes.
  • One reading of a request: route captures, the query string and the body become the spec's arguments by the kernel's rules, and a refusal comes back as DRF's answer with DRF's status.
  • DRF's seats: serializers for input and output, permission classes for authorization, with one serializer context per request.
  • OPTIONS and OpenAPI read off the spec: the opt-in drf-spectacular integration describes each route's request and response.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install django-spec-rest
# or, with uv:
uv add django-spec-rest

The package is not a Django app and needs no INSTALLED_APPS entry. A spec's filter_set needs the kernel's filter extra (pip install "django-service-specs[filter]"), and the OpenAPI integration needs pip install "django-spec-rest[spectacular]".

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: A view or viewset here serves a kernel spec. This page is what happens between the request and the spec: which views take which specs, what the edge reads from the request, how the input is validated, and how each answer and refusal goes back as DRF's. What a spec itself declares is the kernel's documentation.

docs.title: Views and the specs they take
docs.text:
View Spec on spec Methods ServiceCreateView ServiceSpec POST ServiceUpdateView ServiceSpec with a target PUT, PATCH ServiceDeleteView ServiceSpec with a target DELETE SelectorListView SelectorSpec(kind=SelectorKind.LIST) GET SelectorRetrieveView SelectorSpec(kind=SelectorKind.RETRIEVE) GET

ServiceViewSet takes one spec per action in action_specs (list, retrieve, create, update, partial_update, destroy), and SelectorViewSet its list and retrieve; PATCH falls back to update's spec. A custom route takes its spec through @service_action(spec) or @selector_action(spec). See Viewsets and custom actions.

as_view() checks the spec before the view serves anything: a spec of the kind the view does not serve, an update or delete with no target, a nested selector declaring permissions, a filter_set beside DjangoFilterBackend, and what the kernel's seed check refuses of the callables' signatures are each an ImproperlyConfigured at import.

docs.title: What the edge reads from a request
docs.text:
The view turns the request into the one dict of arguments the kernel's dispatch takes, and the principal into request.user:

  • Route captures the spec declares as parameters (reads, or a target selector's reads) are arguments, coerced to their declared type and taken over anything the body or the query string sends for the same name. A capture the spec does not declare is no argument; it stays on view.kwargs for DRF.
  • The query string is read by the kernel's flat reader: a blank value is absent, a typed array or a multiple-choice filter splits on a comma, and each value is coerced to its parameter's type.
  • A JSON body is read as it was sent, and checked against the declared types as sent: a JSON "true" is a string, not a boolean.
  • A form body is read as DRF reads one: "on" and a blank checkbox for a boolean, and the prefixed spellings v.tenant and tags[0] of a nested or list field.
  • A key no parameter declares is dropped, as DRF's serializer drops one.

A write's target is its spec's own: instance_selector_spec for one row, collection_selector_spec for a set. Its reads and its filter_set come from the route and the query string, never the body, so a body value cannot choose the row a write changes. A miss answers 404.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
A spec's SerializerValidator declares the serializer's writable fields as the spec's parameters. The kernel checks the arguments against them first (a missing required field and a mistyped one are refused together), then the serializer validates the body it was bound to: its field validators, validate_<field>() and validate(). The validated data reaches the service as data.

PATCH validates only the fields sent. A spec declaring partial=True validates PUT partially too.

docs.title: Bulk writes
docs.text:
A spec declaring many=True takes a JSON list of rows, each validated by its SerializerValidator, and the service is handed the validated rows as data, a list. A row that fails is refused at the index it was sent at, under the spec's many_argument (items by default), every failing row in one 400, and the service never runs:

from django_service_specs import ServiceSpec, Unrestricted
from rest_framework import serializers

from django_spec_rest import ServiceCreateView
from django_spec_rest.service_specs.serializer_validator import SerializerValidator
from lines.models import Line


def create_lines(*, data):
    return [Line.objects.create(**row) for row in data]


class LineIn(serializers.Serializer):
    sku = serializers.CharField()
    quantity = serializers.IntegerField()


class LinesCreateView(ServiceCreateView):
    spec = ServiceSpec(
        service=create_lines,
        permissions=(Unrestricted(),),
        validator=SerializerValidator(LineIn),
        many=True,
    )

POST /lines/
[{"sku": "a", "quantity": 1}, {"sku": "", "quantity": 1},
 {"sku": "a", "quantity": 1}, {"sku": "", "quantity": 1}]

400 Bad Request
{"items": {"1": {"sku": ["This field may not be blank."]},
           "3": {"sku": ["This field may not be blank."]}}}

A body that is no list is refused as a whole, {"items": ["Expected an array."]}, and so is a list longer than the spec's many_max_length, else the kernel's SERVICE_SPECS_MAX_ARRAY_LENGTH (1000 by default), with a 400 under items. A view taking longer lists declares many_max_length on its spec.

docs.title: Hooks and providers
docs.text:
Three layers feed a write beyond the client's body, the more specific winning on an overlapping key:

Seat View-wide Per action (viewsets) On the spec Extra service keywords get_service_kwargs() get_<action>_service_kwargs() kwargs= provider Extra serializer input get_input_data(request) get_<action>_input_data() input_data= provider Input serializer context get_serializer_context(), then get_input_serializer_context() get_<action>_input_serializer_context() SerializerValidator(serializer_context=) Output serializer context get_serializer_context(), then get_output_serializer_context() get_<action>_output_serializer_context() SerializerPresenter(serializer_context=)

A view hook's value outranks the validated value, so a hook returning {"owner": request.user} cannot be overwritten by a client sending owner. A kwargs provider may not return a key a validator field declares; pass such a value through input_data=, where the serializer validates it. A selector view takes no keyword hook beside a kernel spec: as_view() refuses a get_selector_kwargs override, and the spec's own kwargs provider fills its keywords. See View hooks and providers.

docs.title: Answers
docs.text:
A spec's presenter renders the result. A list view paginates with the view's paginator and presents the page's rows; a list or retrieve spec declaring neither a presenter nor affordances is rendered by the view's serializer_class.

Write Default status create 201 update 200 delete 204

A result with nothing to present answers 204 with no body, and a body never goes out under 204: a value to present answers 200. success_status on the view overrides the default, with an int or a callable declaring any of result, instance, request, view; response_finalizer may replace the response built. as_view() refuses a callable requiring a name the view cannot supply, whether or not it also takes **kwargs, which is handed the names the view has and no others.

docs.title: Refusals
docs.text:
Every refusal leaves as a DRF exception, so DRF's exception handler, and a project's EXCEPTION_HANDLER, answers it as it answers DRF's own:

Refusal Status Body The kernel's InvalidArguments (a missing, mistyped or refused argument) 400 keyed by argument ServiceValidationError 400 its error tree A bare DispatchError 400 {"detail": ...} NotPermitted (a permission check refusing) 403; 401 where a DRF permission class raised NotAuthenticated and DRF answers that with 401 {"detail": ...} PrincipalUnavailable (a deactivated user) 403 {"detail": ...} ServiceNotFound, or a target selector's miss 404 {"detail": ...} ActionUnavailable 409 {"detail": ..., "code": ...} ServiceConflict 409 {"detail": ...} AdditionalInputRequired with a schema 422 {"detail": ..., "schema": ...} any other ServiceError 422 {"detail": ...}

The refusal classes the kernel raises through this package's seats are DRF's as well (DRFInvalidArguments, DRFNotPermitted, ...), so a caller of the kernel's dispatch catches the kernel's class. See DRF seats.

docs.title: OPTIONS
docs.text:
OPTIONS answers DRF's shape (name, description, renders, parses, actions) from the route's specs, and runs no stage of any of them: no selector, provider, service, precondition or affordance condition.

  • Allow names the methods a spec serves, DRF's HEAD beside a GET, and OPTIONS.
  • actions[POST] and actions[PUT] are JSON Schema objects of the spec's parameters, less what the server fills: the keys a seed or a typed provider fills, the route's captures, and on PUT the target lookup's parameters.
  • A method the caller may not send is not described: DRF's permission classes for that method and the kernel's authorize for its spec are both asked, and either refusing leaves it out of actions.

docs.title: Serializer context
docs.text: One context dict is built per request, with request, view, format and action. The input serializer, the output serializer and the service's call_context are handed that same dict, so a key one serializer's validate() writes is there for the service and for the serializer rendering the answer. See Serializer context.

docs.title: Moving from djangorestframework-services
docs.text:
django-spec-rest is djangorestframework-services (drfs) moved onto the kernel, django-service-specs. Its views, viewsets and decorators keep their names; what they serve is now the kernel's own ServiceSpec and SelectorSpec, and DRF enters a spec through three seats: a SerializerValidator, a SerializerPresenter and a DRFPermissionCheck. drfs' own declaration types are gone, and with them every name that re-exported a kernel object.

This page lists what a project moving from drfs 0.62.0 rewrites, and what its clients see change. drfs' history is in its archived changelog.

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
drfs django-spec-rest pip install djangorestframework-services pip install django-spec-rest import rest_framework_services import django_spec_rest "rest_framework_services" in INSTALLED_APPS nothing: the package has no models, templates or app config, so remove the entry the startserviceapp management command none djangorestframework-services[spectacular] django-spec-rest[spectacular]

The package reads no setting of its own. SPEC_REST is reserved as the name of the first one.

docs.title: The import map
docs.text:
The package root exports 29 names, none of them the kernel's. A name drfs re-exported from the kernel is imported from django_service_specs.

drfs spelling Becomes rest_framework_services.<path> for a view, viewset, mixin, decorator or type this package keeps django_spec_rest.<path> ServiceSpec, SelectorSpec, SelectorKind django_service_specs: the kernel's own, declared as below any other kernel name drfs re-exported (ServiceError and its subclasses, Affordance, UNSET, ChangeResult, the relation declarations, PoolSeeds, FieldMarking, FieldAudience, SpecRegistry, create_from_input, update_from_input, apply_input, ...) django_service_specs, from its root can_present_nothing, server_owned_keys, unguarded_specs, resolve_callable_kwargs, audience_projection_for_spec, enforce_affordances, unmet_operation_affordance and their a-prefixed async twins the kernel's functions of the same names, from django_service_specs dispatch_spec, adispatch_spec the kernel's dispatch, adispatch render_spec_output, render_for_audience and their async twins the kernel's present, present_for_audience enforce_permissions the kernel's authorize call_service, call_selector, apply_queryset_shaping and their async twins the kernel's run_service, run_selector, shape_queryset spec_to_json_schema, output_to_json_schema, serializer_to_json_schema the kernel's spec_input_schema and spec_output_schema filterset_to_json_schema the kernel's filter_set_parameters InvalidArguments, NotPermitted, PrincipalUnavailable from service_specs DRFInvalidArguments, DRFNotPermitted, DRFPrincipalUnavailable, each still the kernel's class and DRF's (DRF seats) SerializerValidator, SerializerPresenter, DRFPermissionCheck the same names, under django_spec_rest.service_specs.<module> capability_manifest, build_audience_projection, build_input_serializer, validate_input none: each read a drfs spec

docs.title: Declaring a spec
docs.text:
drfs' ServiceSpec, SelectorSpec, PolymorphicServiceSpec, UrlKwarg, QueryParam, ArgumentBinding, OfflineContract, TargetGuard and the input markers (InputRequired, NotClientInput, InputDescription) are gone. A spec is the kernel's, and each drfs field maps onto one of its seats:

drfs field Kernel spec input_serializer=S validator=SerializerValidator(S) input_serializer_context= SerializerValidator(S, serializer_context=...) output_serializer=S presenter=SerializerPresenter(S) output_serializer_context= SerializerPresenter(S, serializer_context=...) permission_classes=[...] permissions=(DRFPermissionCheck([...]),); a spec that admits everyone says so with the kernel's Unrestricted() reads=[UrlKwarg("pk")], reads=[QueryParam("status")] reads=Parameters.of(Parameter("pk", "integer", required=True)): the edge reads a declared read from the route first, then the query string a QueryParam no callable names shapes=Parameters.of(...) NotClientInput, a hidden lookup key a typed kwargs provider filling the key, which the kernel then keeps out of the caller's arguments (server_owned_keys) PolymorphicServiceSpec one kernel spec per route or action; the polymorphic request body and its {View}_{action}_Request OpenAPI component are gone TargetGuard the kernel's preconditions and object permission, which see the row

JsonSchemaRegistry keeps its fields rules alone. Its filters and python_types rules are gone: a filter_set is described by the kernel's filter_set_parameters, and each read is a Parameter declaring its own type, so a project passing either to extend() or the constructor drops it.

The example project's views declare every seat above.

docs.title: Views and viewsets
docs.text:
• spec and action_specs take kernel specs. @service_action(spec) and @selector_action(spec) take them too. A kernel spec under an action_specs key no action dispatches is refused at as_view(), since its permissions would guard nothing: serve it with a decorator.
  • A write's target is its spec's own selector, never get_object(). An update or delete spec declares instance_selector_spec (one row) or collection_selector_spec (a set) or many=True, and as_view() refuses one that declares none. A get_object() override no longer chooses a write's row.
  • A nested selector declares no permissions. On instance_selector_spec, collection_selector_spec and output_selector_spec the kernel never asks them, so as_view() refuses them: declare them on the spec being served.
  • A selector view's get_selector_kwargs beside a kernel spec is refused at as_view(), with the per-action get_<action>_selector_kwargs: return those keys from the spec's own kwargs provider, which may declare request and view.
  • A viewset's list with a spec never goes through get_queryset(); the view's filter backends and paginator still apply to the set the spec read.
  • success_status and response_finalizer are the view's, read off the class for every action, since a kernel spec declares no HTTP answer.

docs.title: The query string
docs.text:
The query string is read by the kernel's flat reader:

  • A blank filter or a blank declared read is absent. ?status= answers what no parameter answers, where drfs answered 400.
  • A multiple-choice filter splits on a comma and takes a blank: ?st=ann,bob and ?st= answer 200.
  • A typed array splits on a comma: ids=1,2 is [1, 2], and ids=1,,3 answers 400 at the empty element.
  • An array is read no further than one past its cap, and refused with the same 400.
  • A key no parameter declares is dropped, csrfmiddlewaretoken among them. A selector parameter declared only in its signature receives nothing from the query string: declare it in reads.

docs.title: Bodies and arguments
docs.text:
• A form body is read as DRF reads one ("on", a blank checkbox, the prefixed spellings v.tenant and tags[0] of a nested or list field), and a JSON body is checked against the spec's declared types as sent: "true" is no boolean in JSON.
  • A body key named request, view or serializer that no field declares is dropped, as any undeclared key is; it never reaches the seed of that name.
  • A target selector's filter and its reads come from the route and the query string, never the body. On an update or delete a body value cannot choose the row or set the lookup's filter_set scope.
  • A kwargs provider key naming a validator field is refused, pointing at input_data=: a typed provider's when the view is built, an untyped one's on the request whose answer names one. A key named like a field's source stays the provider's.
  • A view hook's value outranks the validated value: a key get_service_kwargs returns that the serializer also declares writable reaches the service as the hook's value, so a client cannot overwrite a hook setting owner=request.user.
  • A provider value named like a filter reaches the filter, over the query string's: the kernel has one argument namespace.
  • The route's format suffix wins for format over a get_serializer_context() override returning its own.

docs.title: Answers
docs.text:
• A bare DispatchError answers 400 with its sentence under detail, where drfs answered 500.
  • A many spec with an output_selector_spec presents what the re-read returns, where drfs presented the service's rows.
  • Bulk and row refusals are worded by the kernel.
  • OPTIONS runs no stage of a spec (no selector, provider, service or affordance condition) and never answers 500. Allow names only the methods a spec serves: a handler with no spec is left out, on its 405 too. actions[METHOD] is a JSON Schema object rather than DRF's per-field dictionary, and leaves out the keys the server fills, the route's captures and the target lookup's parameters. A mixed viewset's methods that no kernel spec serves are no longer described.
  • The browsable API's PUT and PATCH forms are drawn empty, not prefilled from the row: a spec's input need not have the row's fields.
  • OpenAPI describes a filter_set's parameters by the kernel's filter_set_parameters: its description wording, a NumberFilter as a decimal string, an OrderingFilter with no explode or style, in declared order, with maxItems 1000, a MultipleChoiceFilter with maxItems, and an array as a repeated key. A 422 is documented where the spec has a validator. A selector's reads are not documented as query parameters, nor the affordance envelope, nor the null body of an allow_none retrieve.

docs.title: Serializer context
docs.text:
• One context dict per request. The input serializer, the output serializer and the service's call_context are handed the same dict, so a key one serializer's validate() writes is there for the service and the output serializer, as in a stock ModelViewSet. drfs handed each serializer a copy.
  • A presenter's serializer_context callable runs once per row of a list, not once for the page, so a callable that queries runs that query per row.
  • A kernel selector gets no get_<action>_output_serializer_context hook: declare the context on its SerializerPresenter.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
• DRFPermissionCheck takes route_reads= for the arguments that go onto the offline view's kwargs; its url_kwargs= and query_params= are gone, and the offline request's query string is empty.
  • UNAUTHENTICATED_USER = None is passed as None: the principal an anonymous request hands the kernel is None where the project sets it so, rather than an AnonymousUser.

docs.title: Answers kept as they are
docs.text:
• The target lookup runs before the shape check refuses a body key, so a lookup's selector and provider are called for a body the check then refuses.
  • A provider's "abc" or None reaches an x: int selector parameter as returned: a provider is server code, and its values are not coerced.
  • A serializer that cannot be described when the view is built (its get_fields reads context["request"], or a key only the view adds) skips the kernel's seed check at as_view(); its first request is checked instead.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• A kernel spec under @selector_action does not read the view's get_selector_kwargs, and nothing refuses the override there.
  • @service_action does not run the kernel's seed check at as_view().
  • ActionSerializerResolver falls back to the view's serializer_class for an action whose spec has no serializer.
  • A service's ServiceValidationError keyed by a model field is answered under that name, not renamed to the serializer field whose source it is.
  • A kernel dispatch a service makes of the view's own spec for another principal validates under that principal's own context, but its declared parameter set is still the one described under the view's request, until the kernel passes the asking call to parameters().
  • The input serializer is first built with no body and no row, to describe its fields, so one reading self.initial_data or self.instance.<attr> in __init__ or get_fields raises AttributeError on every request, a 500, while as_view() accepts it. Guard the read, as getattr(self, "initial_data", {}) or if self.instance is not None:: the serializer that validates is bound to the body and the row, so a field the guarded read adds there is required and validated.
  • A many spec's row field named like a dispatcher seed, such as user or result, is dropped from each row: refused as missing where it is required, and validated without the value the client sent where it is optional. Name the field otherwise and give it source="user" where the row must still carry that key.
  • The input serializer is built several times per call, to describe its fields as well as to validate, so the queries its __init__ or get_fields makes run several times. Where their count matters, move them to the service, or to validate() or a validate_<field>(), which only the validating build runs.
  • A row condition among a create spec's affordances is refused only when the view dispatches, with ImproperlyConfigured on the first request, not at as_view(). Declare row conditions only on a spec with an instance_selector_spec.

docs.title: Authenticating MCP calls through DRF
docs.text:
django-spec-mcp serves the same kernel specs to agents. Neither package ships a bridge between DRF's authentication and the MCP transport; a project that wants its DRF authentication classes to admit MCP calls writes a backend of its own. The transport calls authenticate(request) with the Django request and expects a TokenInfo, or None for a 401:

from django.http import HttpRequest
from django_spec_mcp import TokenInfo
from django_spec_mcp.auth import bearer_challenge
from django_spec_mcp.auth.types.protected_resource_metadata import ProtectedResourceMetadata
from rest_framework.authentication import TokenAuthentication
from rest_framework.exceptions import APIException
from rest_framework.request import Request


class DRFAuthBackend:
    """Admits an MCP call that the project's DRF authentication classes admit."""

    authentication_classes = (TokenAuthentication,)
    resource_url = "https://example.com/mcp/"

    def authenticate(self, request: HttpRequest) -> TokenInfo | None:
        drf_request = Request(
            request, authenticators=[cls() for cls in self.authentication_classes]
        )
        try:
            user = drf_request.user
        except APIException:
            # An invalid credential: DRF raises AuthenticationFailed.
            return None
        if drf_request.successful_authenticator is None:
            return None
        return TokenInfo(user=user, raw=drf_request.auth)

    def protected_resource_metadata(self) -> ProtectedResourceMetadata:
        return ProtectedResourceMetadata(resource=self.resource_url, authorization_servers=[])

    def www_authenticate_challenge(self, *, scopes=None, error=None) -> str:
        return bearer_challenge(
            resource_metadata_url=f"{self.resource_url}.well-known/oauth-protected-resource",
            scopes=scopes,
            error=error,
        )

Prefer a header-borne credential class (TokenAuthentication, a JWT class): SessionAuthentication enforces CSRF on the transport's POST. Scopes are the transport's to check, with its own scopes=.

docs.title: OpenAPI
docs.text:
The opt-in drf-spectacular integration documents each route from its spec.

pip install "django-spec-rest[spectacular]"

from django.apps import AppConfig


class ApiConfig(AppConfig):
    name = "api"

    def ready(self):
        from django_spec_rest.openapi import enable_openapi

        enable_openapi()

enable_openapi() sets ServiceAutoSchema as the schema of ServiceCreateView, ServiceUpdateView, ServiceDeleteView, SelectorListView, SelectorRetrieveView, ServiceViewSet and SelectorViewSet, so every subclass inherits it; a class setting schema itself keeps its own. Importing django_spec_rest.openapi does not import drf-spectacular; only this call does.

docs.title: What a route documents
docs.text:
• The request body is a SerializerValidator's serializer, under drf-spectacular's component name for the class, built partial where the route validates partially (a PATCH, or a spec declaring partial). A many spec takes a list of its rows. Any other validator is the kernel's JSON Schema of the parameters the body carries.
  • The response body is a SerializerPresenter's serializer, or another presenter's output schema, a list where the spec presents rows. A spec with no presenter documents no content; a selector spec with none keeps the view's serializer_class, which renders it.
  • The status is the view's success_status where it is an int, over the action's default. A body documented under 204 is documented as the 200 it is served as, with a 204 beside it where the spec can present nothing.
  • A 422 is documented wherever the spec declares a validator.
  • A filter_set's query parameters, on a list operation, are the kernel's filter_set_parameters.

ServiceErrorSerializer, a single detail field, is the body of that 422, under the ServiceError component.

User-supplied @extend_schema annotations always win, and @extend_schema(parameters=...) merges over the filter parameters as it does for a view-level FilterSet.

docs.title: Not documented
docs.text: A selector spec's declared reads are not documented as query parameters, nor the affordance envelope a spec declaring affordances renders, nor the null body of an allow_none retrieve. Add them with @extend_schema where a client needs them.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: A resource served on a viewset: list, retrieve, create and update an invoice. The example project is this page, finished and tested.

docs.title: 1. Services and selectors
docs.text:
Plain callables. A service names the values it needs by keyword: data is the validated input, instance the row a write targets. A refusal is one of the kernel's errors, which the view answers with its HTTP status.

from django_service_specs import ServiceConflict

from invoices.models import Invoice


def create_invoice(*, data):
    return Invoice.objects.create(**data)


def update_invoice(*, instance, data):
    if instance.status != Invoice.STATUS_DRAFT:
        raise ServiceConflict("Only a draft invoice can be changed.")  # 409
    for name, value in data.items():
        setattr(instance, name, value)
    instance.save()
    return instance


def list_invoices():
    return Invoice.objects.all()


def get_invoice(*, pk):
    return Invoice.objects.filter(pk=pk).first()  # None answers 404

docs.title: 2. Serializers
docs.text:
Ordinary DRF serializers: one validates a body, one renders a row.

from rest_framework import serializers


class InvoiceInput(serializers.Serializer):
    customer = serializers.CharField(max_length=200)
    amount_cents = serializers.IntegerField(min_value=0)
    notes = serializers.CharField(required=False, allow_blank=True)


class InvoiceSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    class Meta:
        model = Invoice
        fields = ("id", "customer", "amount_cents", "notes", "status")

docs.title: 3. Specs
docs.text:
Each spec is the kernel's. The serializers fill its validator and presenter seats. The kernel refuses to dispatch a spec that declares no permissions; Unrestricted() says the operation is open to every caller.

from django_service_specs import (
    Parameter,
    Parameters,
    SelectorKind,
    SelectorSpec,
    ServiceSpec,
    Unrestricted,
)

from django_spec_rest.service_specs.serializer_presenter import SerializerPresenter
from django_spec_rest.service_specs.serializer_validator import SerializerValidator

OPEN = (Unrestricted(),)
PRESENTER = SerializerPresenter(InvoiceSerializer)
BY_PK = Parameters.of(Parameter("pk", "integer", required=True))

LIST_SPEC = SelectorSpec(
    kind=SelectorKind.LIST, selector=list_invoices, permissions=OPEN, presenter=PRESENTER
)
RETRIEVE_SPEC = SelectorSpec(
    kind=SelectorKind.RETRIEVE,
    selector=get_invoice,
    reads=BY_PK,
    permissions=OPEN,
    presenter=PRESENTER,
)
CREATE_SPEC = ServiceSpec(
    service=create_invoice,
    validator=SerializerValidator(InvoiceInput),
    permissions=OPEN,
    presenter=PRESENTER,
)
UPDATE_SPEC = ServiceSpec(
    service=update_invoice,
    validator=SerializerValidator(InvoiceInput),
    # The row an update writes is found by its own selector, reading ``pk``
    # from the route. A nested selector declares no permissions.
    instance_selector_spec=SelectorSpec(
        kind=SelectorKind.RETRIEVE, selector=get_invoice, reads=BY_PK
    ),
    permissions=OPEN,
    presenter=PRESENTER,
)

docs.title: 4. The viewset and its routes
docs.text:
from rest_framework.routers import DefaultRouter

from django_spec_rest import ServiceViewSet


class InvoiceViewSet(ServiceViewSet):
    action_specs = {
        "list": LIST_SPEC,
        "retrieve": RETRIEVE_SPEC,
        "create": CREATE_SPEC,
        "update": UPDATE_SPEC,  # PATCH falls back to it, validated partially
    }


router = DefaultRouter()
router.register("invoices", InvoiceViewSet, basename="invoice")
urlpatterns = router.urls

That serves:

Request Answer GET /invoices/ the rows, rendered by InvoiceSerializer GET /invoices/1/ one row, or 404 POST /invoices/ 201 with the created row, or 400 keyed by field PUT /invoices/1/ every required field validated PATCH /invoices/1/ only the fields sent validated; 409 for a sent invoice DELETE /invoices/1/ 405: no spec serves it, and Allow leaves it out OPTIONS /invoices/1/ the PUT body as a JSON Schema, with no stage of a spec run

docs.title: 5. The same spec off HTTP
docs.text:
A spec is not tied to its route. The kernel's dispatch runs it for a principal and a dict of arguments:

from django_service_specs import dispatch

result = dispatch(
    UPDATE_SPEC,
    principal=user,
    arguments={"pk": 1, "customer": "Acme Ltd", "amount_cents": 4200},
)
result.value  # the updated Invoice

See Calling a spec off HTTP.

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text:
Task-shaped how-tos. Each assumes the Quickstart and Concepts. What a spec itself declares (preconditions, affordances, queryset shaping, nested relations, bulk writes, a spec registry shared by several transports) is the kernel's documentation.

  • Viewsets and custom actions: action_specs, @service_action, @selector_action, and composing a viewset from the per-action mixins.
  • View hooks and providers: the server's values for a service, on the spec and on the view, and which outranks which.
  • DRF permission classes: DRFPermissionCheck on a spec, over HTTP and off it.
  • Filter a selector with filter_set: a django-filter FilterSet read off the query string.
  • Serializer context: one context dict per request, and the keys a spec or a view adds.
  • Calling a spec off HTTP: the kernel's dispatch over a spec a route serves.

docs.title: View hooks and providers
docs.text: A service is handed the keywords it declares: the kernel's seeds (user, data, instance, request, view, ...), the spec's arguments, and the values the server adds. The server adds them in two places: on the spec, which every transport serving it runs, and on the view, which only HTTP runs.

docs.title: On the spec: providers
docs.text:
A kwargs provider returns extra keywords for the service; an input_data provider returns values merged into the input before the serializer validates it. Either declares the seeds it reads: user is the principal on every transport, and over HTTP request and view are the call's.

from django_service_specs import ServiceSpec


def tenant_kwargs(*, user):
    return {"tenant": user.tenant}


CREATE_SPEC = ServiceSpec(
    service=create_note,  # def create_note(*, data, tenant): ...
    validator=SerializerValidator(NoteInput),
    kwargs=tenant_kwargs,
    permissions=OPEN,
)

A kwargs provider may not return a key a validator field declares: its value would reach the service unvalidated. A typed provider (one whose return annotation is a TypedDict) naming such a key is refused when the view is built, and an untyped one on the request whose answer names it. Return the value from input_data= instead, where the serializer validates it. A key named like a field's source stays the provider's.

A provider is server code, and its values reach the callable as returned: a provider's "abc" for an x: int parameter is not coerced.

docs.title: On the view: hooks
docs.text:
A mutation view or viewset has three hook chains, view-wide then per action, the more specific winning on a key both return, and the spec's provider over both:

Hook Feeds get_service_kwargs(), get_<action>_service_kwargs() the service's keywords get_input_data(request), get_<action>_input_data() the input, before validation get_input_serializer_context(), get_<action>_input_serializer_context() the input serializer's context 
from django_spec_rest import ServiceViewSet


class NoteViewSet(ServiceViewSet):
    action_specs = {"create": CREATE_SPEC}

    def get_service_kwargs(self):
        return {"owner": self.request.user}

A hook's value outranks the client's. Where the serializer declares a writable owner, the hook's value is what reaches the service, so a client sending owner cannot replace the hook's. A key a validate() derives, or a source="*" nested serializer flattens, reaches the service's keyword as the hook's value, while data keeps what the serializer validated.

A selector view takes no keyword hook beside a kernel spec: as_view() refuses a get_selector_kwargs or get_<action>_selector_kwargs override, which would never reach the spec. Return those keys from the spec's kwargs provider.

Prefer the spec's providers for anything the operation needs wherever it is served: a hook runs over HTTP only, and the same spec dispatched through the kernel's dispatch, or served on another transport, never asks it.

docs.title: Calling a spec off HTTP
docs.text:
A spec served on a route is the kernel's, so the kernel's dispatch runs it with no request: from a management command, a task, a test, or another transport serving kernel specs.

from django_service_specs import dispatch

result = dispatch(
    UPDATE_SPEC,
    principal=user,
    arguments={"pk": invoice.pk, "customer": "Acme Ltd", "amount_cents": 4200},
)
result.value  # what the service returned

docs.title: Arguments in place of a request
docs.text:
There is no route, query string or body: arguments holds every value the spec declares. A value the route would have captured, such as the pk a target selector reads, is an argument like any other. A key no parameter declares is refused under the kernel's default, where the HTTP edge drops it.

The input is validated as declared: the kernel checks the arguments' types, then the SerializerValidator's serializer validates them. Nothing is partial unless the spec declares partial=True; a PATCH route's partial validation is the route's.

docs.title: What runs and what does not
docs.text:
• The spec's own seats run: its providers, permissions, preconditions, validator and service. result.value is what the service returned; the kernel's present renders it through the spec's presenter.
  • The view does not: its permission_classes, its hooks (get_service_kwargs, get_input_data, the serializer context hooks), success_status and response_finalizer belong to the route. Put what the operation needs everywhere on the spec.

A kernel dispatch a service makes for another principal runs under that principal's offline request and view as well: neither the outer request nor the view reaches its validation or the description of its serializer.

docs.title: DRF's seats without a request
docs.text:
• DRFPermissionCheck asks its classes against an offline request and view built for the principal; see DRF permission classes.
  • A serializer's context is built over the same offline pair, so self.context["request"].user is the principal; see Serializer context.
  • A refusal is the kernel's class: DRFNotPermitted, DRFInvalidArguments and the other DRF refusal classes subclass the kernel's, so except NotPermitted catches a DRF permission class's refusal.

The example project dispatches its update spec and its permission-checked send spec this way.

docs.title: DRF permission classes
docs.text: A route is guarded twice, in order: the view's own permission_classes, which DRF asks in initial() before any handler runs, and the spec's permissions, which the kernel's dispatch asks. The view's classes guard the route; the spec's guard the operation, wherever it is served.

docs.title: On the spec: DRFPermissionCheck
docs.text:
from django_service_specs import ServiceSpec
from rest_framework.permissions import IsAuthenticated

from django_spec_rest.service_specs.drf_permission_check import DRFPermissionCheck

SEND_SPEC = ServiceSpec(
    service=send_invoice,
    instance_selector_spec=INVOICE_LOOKUP,
    permissions=(DRFPermissionCheck([IsAuthenticated]),),
    presenter=PRESENTER,
)

DRFPermissionCheck asks every class in order, a fresh instance each time, as DRF's get_permissions does:

  • has_permission against the request and view the call carries. A refusal raises DRFNotPermitted with that class's own message and code, which DRF answers 403. A class raising DRF's NotAuthenticated leaves as DRFNotAuthenticated, which DRF answers 401 where the authenticator supplies a challenge.
  • has_object_permission of the row a write targets or a retrieve finds, when it is a model instance.
  • The kernel's question about a set (a bulk call, a collection, a create) is allowed: DRF has no such question, and the class-level check has already run.

Each refusal is the kernel's NotPermitted as well, so a caller of the kernel's dispatch catches it by the kernel's class.

docs.title: Off HTTP
docs.text:
The same check runs when the spec is dispatched with no request. It builds an offline request and view for the principal (build_offline_context), so a class reading request.user reads the principal, and view.action is the call context's action where one is given. The offline request's query string is empty.

A class scoping by a route capture reads view.kwargs, which off HTTP no URLconf fills. Name those arguments in route_reads, and the check puts them on the offline view's kwargs before asking:

DRFPermissionCheck([IsProjectMember], route_reads=["project_pk"])

from django_service_specs import NotPermitted, dispatch

dispatch(SEND_SPEC, principal=user, arguments={"pk": invoice.pk})  # runs
dispatch(SEND_SPEC, principal=AnonymousUser(), arguments={"pk": invoice.pk})  # NotPermitted

The example project asserts both, and the 403 over HTTP.

docs.title: A nested selector declares none
docs.text: The specs on instance_selector_spec, collection_selector_spec and output_selector_spec are never asked for their permissions: the spec being served is what authorizes. as_view() refuses a nested selector that declares permissions, so a check placed there cannot look like it guards something.

docs.title: Filter a selector with filter_set
docs.text:
A kernel SelectorSpec takes a django-filter FilterSet on filter_set. The kernel applies it to the queryset the selector returns, with the FilterSet's filters as the spec's arguments, so the same filters apply over HTTP, off HTTP and on any other transport. It needs the kernel's filter extra:

pip install "django-service-specs[filter]"

import django_filters
from django_service_specs import SelectorKind, SelectorSpec


class InvoiceFilter(django_filters.FilterSet):
    status = django_filters.ChoiceFilter(choices=Invoice.STATUS_CHOICES)
    customer = django_filters.CharFilter(lookup_expr="icontains")

    class Meta:
        model = Invoice
        fields = []


LIST_SPEC = SelectorSpec(
    kind=SelectorKind.LIST,
    selector=list_invoices,
    filter_set=InvoiceFilter,
    permissions=OPEN,
    presenter=PRESENTER,
)

docs.title: Over HTTP
docs.text:
A list route reads the filters off the query string, by the kernel's flat reader:

Request Answer GET /invoices/?status=sent the sent invoices GET /invoices/?customer=acm the invoices whose customer contains acm GET /invoices/?status= every invoice: a blank filter is absent GET /invoices/?status=lost 400, keyed status

A multiple-choice filter takes repeated keys or one comma-separated value (?st=ann,bob), and a typed array splits on a comma.

filter_set replaces DjangoFilterBackend: a list view declaring both is refused at as_view(), since the queryset would be filtered twice. The view's other filter backends, and its paginator, still apply to the set the spec read.

docs.title: Values the server supplies
docs.text: The kernel has one argument namespace, so a kwargs provider's value named like a filter reaches the filter, over the query string's. That is the place for a scope the client must not choose.

docs.title: A write's target
docs.text: A filter_set on an update's or a delete's instance_selector_spec or collection_selector_spec reads the route and the query string only, never the body: a body value cannot set the scope that picks the row a write changes.

docs.title: A retrieve
docs.text: A retrieve spec runs its own selector rather than DRF's get_object(), so the view's filter_backends do not apply to it: a tenant-scoping backend in DEFAULT_FILTER_BACKENDS narrows the list and not the lookup. Scope the selector's queryset, or declare the rule as the spec's filter_set.

docs.title: One dict per request
docs.text:
Over HTTP the view builds one context dict per request, holding DRF's request, view and format, the viewset's action, and every key the view's get_serializer_context() adds. The input serializer, the output serializer and the service's call_context are all handed that same dict, as one serializer validating and rendering in a stock ModelViewSet sees one context:

from rest_framework import serializers


class InvoiceInput(serializers.Serializer):
    amount_cents = serializers.IntegerField(min_value=0)

    def validate(self, attrs):
        if attrs["amount_cents"] == 0:
            self.context.setdefault("warnings", []).append("The amount is zero.")
        return attrs


class InvoiceSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    warnings = serializers.SerializerMethodField()

    def get_warnings(self, invoice):
        return list(self.context.get("warnings", []))


def create_invoice(*, data, call_context):
    call_context.get("warnings")  # the same list

The example project asserts the warning validate() writes is rendered in the answer.

format is the route's: on a route with a format suffix, format is the suffix even where an overriding get_serializer_context() answers another value for it.

docs.title: Keys a spec adds
docs.text:
SerializerValidator(serializer_context=...) and SerializerPresenter(serializer_context=...) take a callable returning keys for their serializer. Over HTTP the validator's keys are written into the request's one dict, so the service and the output serializer see them too.

CREATE_SPEC = ServiceSpec(
    service=create_invoice,
    validator=SerializerValidator(InvoiceInput, serializer_context=lambda: {"currency": "EUR"}),
    presenter=SerializerPresenter(InvoiceSerializer),
    permissions=OPEN,
)

A presenter's serializer_context callable runs once for each row it renders, so for a list it runs once per row, not once for the page: a callable that queries runs its query per row. Load what every row needs in the selector (select_related, prefetch_related, annotations) instead.

docs.title: Keys a view adds
docs.text:
A mutation view's hooks layer keys over DRF's context, view-wide then per action:

Serializer View-wide Per action input get_input_serializer_context() get_<action>_input_serializer_context() output get_output_serializer_context() get_<action>_output_serializer_context()

Both view-wide hooks default to get_serializer_context(). A selector spec's presenter is not handed the per-action output hook: declare its context on its SerializerPresenter.

docs.title: Off HTTP
docs.text: Dispatched with no request, a seat builds its serializer over an offline request and view for the principal, so a serializer reading self.context["request"].user while it validates reads the principal. Off HTTP the kernel also describes the serializer's fields before the call, with no request in its context: a get_fields() or __init__ reading self.context["request"] raises there, so guard such a read. base_serializer_context and build_offline_context build that context for code of your own that renders a serializer outside a view.

docs.title: The standard actions
docs.text:
ServiceViewSet serves list, retrieve, create, update, partial_update and destroy, each from its entry in action_specs. SelectorViewSet serves list and retrieve. An action with no entry falls back to DRF's own behaviour for the reads (get_queryset(), get_object()) and answers 405 for the writes, and Allow leaves an unserved write out.

from django_spec_rest import ServiceViewSet


class InvoiceViewSet(ServiceViewSet):
    action_specs = {
        "list": LIST_SPEC,
        "retrieve": RETRIEVE_SPEC,
        "create": CREATE_SPEC,
        "update": UPDATE_SPEC,
        # "partial_update" is optional: PATCH falls back to "update",
        # validated partially. Declare it to give PATCH a spec of its own,
        # or alone for a PATCH-only route.
    }

An entry under list or retrieve must be a SelectorSpec, and under a write key a ServiceSpec. An entry under a key no action dispatches is refused at as_view(), since nothing would ask its permissions: a custom route takes its spec through a decorator.

docs.title: A custom write: @service_action
docs.text:
from typing import Any

from django_spec_rest import ServiceViewSet, service_action


class InvoiceViewSet(ServiceViewSet):
    action_specs = {...}

    @service_action(SEND_SPEC, detail=True, methods=["post"])
    def send(self, request: Any, pk: Any = None) -> None:
        """Mark a draft as sent."""

The method's body never runs: the decorator supplies the handler, and the method gives DRF's @action its name. detail, methods, url_path, url_name and any other keyword go to DRF's @action. On a detail route the row is the spec's own target selector's, read from the route's pk, never get_object()'s. The answer is the spec's presenter's, under the viewset's success_status (200 by default).

docs.title: A custom read: @selector_action
docs.text:
from django_spec_rest import SelectorViewSet, selector_action


class InvoiceViewSet(SelectorViewSet):
    @selector_action(OVERDUE_SPEC)
    def overdue(self, request: Any) -> None:
        """Invoices past their due date."""

The spec's kind sets the route's shape: a LIST spec is a collection action, paginated where the viewset paginates, and a RETRIEVE spec a detail action, answering 404 for a miss or null under allow_none.

docs.title: Composing your own viewset
docs.text:
Each standard action is a mixin over GenericViewSet, so a viewset takes only the actions it serves:

from rest_framework.viewsets import GenericViewSet

from django_spec_rest import (
    ActionSerializerResolver,
    SelectorListMixin,
    ServiceCreateMixin,
)


class InboxViewSet(ServiceCreateMixin, SelectorListMixin, ActionSerializerResolver, GenericViewSet):
    action_specs = {"list": INBOX_SPEC, "create": POST_MESSAGE_SPEC}

ActionSerializerResolver answers get_serializer_class() per action: a write spec's input serializer where the viewset sets no serializer_class, which DRF's browsable API asks to draw its forms, and the viewset's serializer_class otherwise.

docs.title: A standalone view
docs.text:
A single route needs no viewset:

from django_spec_rest import SelectorListView


class SentInvoiceListView(SelectorListView):
    spec = SENT_SPEC

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
Autodocumented public API. Every page reads the docstrings and signatures from the source.

A spec itself, and everything the kernel owns (ServiceSpec, SelectorSpec, Parameter, Parameters, SelectorKind, the refusals, dispatch), is imported from django_service_specs and documented there. This package documents what it adds over DRF.

  • Views: ServiceCreateView, ServiceUpdateView, ServiceDeleteView, SelectorListView, SelectorRetrieveView, MutationFlowMixin, resolve_mutation_instance.
  • Viewsets: ServiceViewSet, SelectorViewSet, the per-action mixins, ActionSerializerResolver, @service_action, @selector_action.
  • DRF seats: SerializerValidator, SerializerPresenter, DRFPermissionCheck, the DRF refusal classes and the translators between the kernel's refusals and DRF's, and the offline context.
  • Types: ServiceView, ViewHooks, HttpExtras, the offline request and view, MARKING and the JSON Schema registry.
  • OpenAPI: enable_openapi, ServiceAutoSchema, ServiceErrorSerializer (the opt-in drf-spectacular adapter).

docs.title: Public surface
docs.text:
The top-level django_spec_rest package exports the 29 names below. The subpackages django_spec_rest.views, django_spec_rest.viewsets, django_spec_rest.types and django_spec_rest.openapi export theirs from their __init__, and the seat adapters are imported from their leaf modules under django_spec_rest.service_specs, as the DRF seats page shows.

Group Names Views ServiceCreateView, ServiceUpdateView, ServiceDeleteView, SelectorListView, SelectorRetrieveView, MutationFlowMixin, resolve_mutation_instance Viewsets ServiceViewSet, SelectorViewSet, ServiceCreateMixin, ServiceUpdateMixin, ServiceDestroyMixin, SelectorListMixin, SelectorRetrieveMixin, ActionSerializerResolver, service_action, selector_action Types ServiceView, ViewHooks, HttpExtras, OfflineContext, OfflineHttpRequest, OfflineServiceView, MARKING, JsonSchemaRegistry, DEFAULT_JSON_SCHEMA_REGISTRY Serializer helpers base_serializer_context, build_offline_context, renderable_serializer_class

docs.title: enable_openapi
docs.text:
enable_openapi() -> None

Set ServiceAutoSchema as the schema on every library view class.

Call once from AppConfig.ready() (or anywhere after Django apps are loaded) to make drf-spectacular see a spec's request bodies, response bodies, success statuses, and 422 contracts, a kernel ServiceSpec or SelectorSpec read off its Validator and presenter, on:

  • ServiceCreateView, ServiceUpdateView, ServiceDeleteView
  • SelectorListView, SelectorRetrieveView
  • ServiceViewSet, SelectorViewSet

The function-local imports keep drf-spectacular an optional dependency: importing django_spec_rest.openapi does not require it, and only this call brings in the schema-generator code.

User subclasses inherit schema = ServiceAutoSchema() automatically; classes that set schema = ... explicitly keep their own choice.

docs.title: ServiceAutoSchema
docs.text:
Bases: AutoSchema

AutoSchema that derives its request / response from a kernel spec.

A kernel ServiceSpec or SelectorSpec is read off its seats, as the route serves it, on every surface: the standalone Service*View and Selector*View classes, the ServiceViewSet and SelectorViewSet action mixins, and @service_action / @selector_action:

  • The request body is a SerializerValidator's serializer, so its component is drf-spectacular's name for the author's class, built partial exactly where the route dispatches the spec's partial variant (kernel_spec_variant): a PATCH, unless the Validator cannot take a partial call, and a spec declaring partial. A many spec takes a list of those rows. Any other Validator is the kernel's parameters_schema over what the body carries (_parameters_body).
  • The response body is a SerializerPresenter's serializer, or any other presenter's output_schema, a list of rows where the spec presents rows (_presents_rows). A spec with no presenter documents the no-content response, and a selector spec with none keeps the base's reading of the view's serializer_class, which renders it.
  • The status is the view's success_status where it is an int, since a kernel spec declares none, over the action's default; a body is documented as the 200 it is served as where that is 204, and the 204 beside it where can_present_nothing.
  • A 422 is documented wherever the spec declares a Validator.
  • A FilterSet's query parameters are the kernel's filter_set_parameters, on a list operation only.

User-supplied @extend_schema annotations always win, and @extend_schema(parameters=...) merges over the filter parameters exactly as it does for a view-level FilterSet.

docs.title: ServiceErrorSerializer
docs.text:
Bases: Serializer

Single-field detail serializer that mirrors _ServiceAPIException.

Used by ServiceAutoSchema to attach a 422 response to every spec-driven mutation in the generated OpenAPI document. It is only used for schema generation; runtime 422 bodies are produced by DRF's exception handler from _ServiceAPIException.

docs.title: DRF seats
docs.text:
A kernel spec has three seats DRF can fill: its validator, its presenter and its permissions. This page is the adapters that fill them, the DRF refusal classes the kernel's refusals become, and the helpers a caller off HTTP uses to give a serializer the context it reads.

None of these is exported from the package root; import each from its leaf module:

from django_spec_rest.service_specs.drf_permission_check import DRFPermissionCheck
from django_spec_rest.service_specs.serializer_presenter import SerializerPresenter
from django_spec_rest.service_specs.serializer_validator import SerializerValidator

docs.title: SerializerValidator
docs.text:
Bases: Validator

A Validator whose declaration is a DRF serializer, or a dataclass read through one.

It takes a Serializer subclass, ModelSerializer and DataclassSerializer included, or a dataclass, which is validated through a DataclassSerializer built for it. Anything else is refused with ImproperlyConfigured when the Validator is built.

parameters() walks the serializer's fields, in order, as the field walk in service_specs/utils.py reads them: a nested serializer is an object with Parameters of its own, many=True and a ListField an array, a file field a file, choices with their labels; a HiddenField and a read-only field are no parameter. It is read on each call rather than when the Validator is built, because specs are built at import time, when a ModelSerializer cannot yet read its model, and so that help is rendered in the language active when it is asked for. It never queries.

validate() builds the serializer as a DRF view would:

  • over the body the call was sent, where a DRF edge call names this Validator (validator_input): the caller's own data, a QueryDict kept one, with what the edge put over it, as a DRF view's serializer was always handed request.data. Anywhere else, the kernel's checked arguments.

  • with the target as instance, so an update's uniqueness checks exclude the row being updated. The queryset a collection selector resolves is no row, so a call over one binds as a create; the target is handed over as it is, since a serializer, unlike a ModelForm, writes nothing onto its instance while it validates.

  • partial as the call is, the context's partial, so a partial call may leave out a required field and returns only what was sent.
  • under the serializer context DRF builds on HTTP, request, format and view. The request and view the call registered as pool seeds are the serializer's own, read from ValidationContext.ambient as the kernel resolved them, and where a seed is absent or None, the entry of that name in ValidationContext.call_context. A call that carries neither gets an offline request whose user is the principal and whose data is the arguments, built by build_offline_context, so a CurrentUserDefault reads the principal and a field or a validate() reading self.context["request"] finds a request rather than a KeyError. What a registered request's user is, is the transport's to make the principal; the Validator never writes to a call's own objects. Over that, the input half of the view hooks a DRF edge carries for the call (input_view_layers), then this Validator's own serializer_context, each winning on a key it shares with what it layers over (see serializer_context in service_specs/utils.py). The callable declares what it reads from the call's pool: request, view, user, call_context, a registered seed, or an argument. It is asked once per call, a many call's included, except where the call builds the serializer twice, for a body the server puts a value into or a row a target lookup resolves, and what the callable is handed differs between the two.

A refusal is one DRFInvalidArguments, the kernel's refusal that is DRF's ValidationError as well, carrying the serializer's errors unchanged: DRF's ErrorDetail leaves, each with its code, cross-field messages under non_field_errors, and a nested list's errors in whichever shape the installed DRF writes them.

validated() hands the service data, the serializer's validated_data - the validated mapping, or the dataclass instance a DataclassSerializer builds - and the bound serializer is bound for the call as serializer. values follow what validated_data is: a mapping's entries, keyed as DRF keys them, by each field's source; a dataclass instance's __init__ fields, whether a dataclass was declared or a DataclassSerializer subclass was; and nothing for any other object a serializer's validate() returns, which reaches the service only as data. A key named like a seed of the call is a value only in data: DRF's HiddenField(default=CurrentUserDefault()) named user, or a key a validate() adds named result, stays in validated_data as the serializer built it, and the service's user is the call's principal (see _unseeded). So is a key named in server_owned, the names the caller declares the server's: the client's value is the service's in data alone, unless the edge put the server's value into the field it comes from (see _unowned). Where the edge did, that field's validation of the value the edge put is the key's value, validated on its own once the serializer has accepted the body, never read back off the body (see _server_values), whatever the field reads from the body, and whatever a later field of the same source, a source="*" nested serializer, a validate() or a to_internal_value override did to the key: it is the parameter's, by the field's source or, where that is no single key, by the field's name, and by the key an author named it under (see _handed), and it is laid back over the key in a mapping data (see _lay_back). A dataclass instance is data as built, and a many call's rows are neither validated apart nor laid back.

A partial call over a dataclass is refused, a DataclassSerializer subclass included: one builds its instance from every field, and a field a partial call left out fails as a TypeError from inside the library. supports_partial is therefore answered per instance, False for either declaration and True for any other serializer, so a spec declaring partial=True over a dataclass is refused when it is built. A partial call made on the Validator directly is refused with ImproperlyConfigured as well.

validated_many() validates a many spec's rows as DRF's own list serializer does, once: the serializer's child class under many=True (so a Meta.list_serializer_class and its list-level validate() run), with the call's context and partial flag. The one list serializer is bound for the call as serializer, data is the list of each row's validated_data and the values are the rows' values under many_argument. A refusal is an DRFInvalidArguments whose detail keys each failing row by the index the caller's list gave it, whichever of DRF's two shapes the installed version reports item errors in, and whose list-level message sits under non_field_errors. Over HTTP as off it, the list bound is the rows the kernel passed: where it refused a row, the list's own checks judge the rows left, and their refusal sits beside the refused row's (test_bulk_rows_over_http's test_a_lists_own_checks_judge_the_rows_the_kernel_passed).

unsendable: frozenset[str]

The required input fields no call on the kernel route can send.

A field named like a seed (RESERVED_POOL_SEEDS, BOUND or excluded) is no parameter (see parameters()), so the kernel has nowhere to take its value from, while an HTTP body carries it by name. Where the serializer requires such a field, a call through the kernel's dispatch is refused for it however it is made. This names those fields, by the name parameters() would have declared them under, so a transport can refuse such a spec before a call reaches it::

compiled.validator.unsendable
  • Only what parameters() omits. A field the Validator declares a parameter for is never named, even one a seed, a server argument or a call seed then fills: a field named like a registered seed is one unless the caller names it in excluded. A required field called serializer or user is named.
  • Required only. An optional field, one with a default, a read_only field and a HiddenField are no input to require (test_an_optional_field_is_not_unsendable, test_a_read_only_field_is_not_unsendable, test_a_hidden_field_is_not_unsendable), and a many spec's row fields are read through the row serializer this Validator holds, so a row's required user is named and a row's tenant is not (test_a_many_specs_row_fields_are_read_through_the_row_serializer).

docs.title: SerializerPresenter
docs.text:
Bases: Presenter

An operation's output declared as a DRF serializer, rendered through it.

output() reads the serializer's fields into the kernel's Output, in declaration order:

  • A write_only field is never rendered, so it is not declared.
  • Type: JSON's own, with decimal, date-time and date as formats. A nested serializer is an object carrying its own Output; a many=True serializer, and a ListField whose child is one, is an array of that Output; a MultipleChoiceField is an array of its choices. A field DRF gives no type, a SerializerMethodField or a JSONField say, is declared any, so a schema describes it with no type rather than as a string it may not be.
  • Label: the author's, when one was written. DRF derives Vat id from vat_id when none was, and that is None here: a derived label says nothing the name does not.
  • Choices: every (value, display) pair a ChoiceField holds, typed by the values when they share a type.
  • Presence: always_present is true where DRF is bound to emit the key: a required field, one with a default, and one allowing null. A read-only field with neither is dropped when DRF cannot read it. Under shaped=True, no field at any depth is: the spec compiles a shape, an argument such as a fields selector that the serializer reads off the request, and a key is always present only if it is present under every value the caller may send. Such an argument declares no choices, so the values are any string, and which keys each one drops is the serializer's to decide when it renders, so the keys present under all of them are none that can be named. The default, False, is the presence above.
  • Marking: the FieldMarking found in the field's style, under MARKING or any other key, and a value under MARKING that is not one refused. Nested outputs carry their own.

field_audiences is the spec's own output declaration, a field name to a FieldMarking, layered over the serializer's markings at the top level only. The layered marking is the compiled OutputField.marking, which is the seat audience_projection_for_spec reads, so every engine projects the one declaration with no overrides=, which stays a mount's. A name that is no output field is refused when the output is read: a hidden marking that silently applies to nothing is a field shown to an agent.

presented(value, context) is what the kernel's present asks for: the serializer's .data for one value, under the serializer context derived from the call's PresentationContext. The request and view the call registered as pool seeds, read from ambient, are the serializer's own, and where a seed is absent or None, the entry of that name in call_context; a call that carries neither gets an offline request whose user is the principal, so a SerializerMethodField reading self.context["request"].user renders for the principal the call ran for, and whose query string is the call's shapes, so a serializer reading a fields selector off request.query_params finds the one the caller sent. A request the call carries is left as it is. A list result is presented row by row by the kernel's present, each row with the same context, which is what a many=True render is. Over that, the output half of the view hooks a DRF edge adds to the result's context (output_view_layers), resolved with the value, then this Presenter's own serializer_context, each winning on a key it shares with what it layers over (see serializer_context in service_specs/utils.py). The callable declares what it reads from the call's pool, request, view, user or a registered seed, and the value being presented under value_keyword: result for a service's output, instance for a retrieve. It is asked once per value presented, so for a list or a many service's output once per row, and no keyword names the row then (value_keyword is None), nor is the view's hook handed it: the kernel presents a set row by row, and the whole set a callable may declare, a list's page or a many output's result, is never in hand here.

present(value) is the context-free form, and delegates to presented(value, None): a None context is the serializer context a serializer is described with outside any call (request, view and format present, each None), so a get_fields reading self.context["request"] neither raises there nor sees a principal. It is what a DispatchResult a transport built by hand is presented with, and with no call to resolve it against, serializer_context is not asked (test_present_with_no_call_runs_no_callable).

A dataclass type is read and rendered through a DataclassSerializer built for it, and a BaseSerializer that is not a Serializer declares no fields, so its output is empty while it still presents.

docs.title: DRFPermissionCheck
docs.text:
Bases: PermissionCheck

DRF permission classes asked the kernel's three questions, off HTTP.

The kernel asks a principal and a spec; a DRF permission class asks a request and a view. So each question asks every class in order, a fresh instance each time, as a DRF view's get_permissions does, against the request and view the call carries, else the offline pair build_offline_context builds for the principal. The first refusal raises the dual-base DRFNotPermitted with that class's own message and code, so a client is told what a DRF view would have told it; returning False instead would leave the kernel to raise its own class with the generic wording. A class that raises its own refusal is asked inside translate_drf_refusals, so DRF's PermissionDenied leaves as that DRFNotPermitted with the class's message and code, and NotAuthenticated as DRFNotAuthenticated, which DRF still answers 401 (tests/service_specs/test_drf_refusals_on_the_kernel_route.py).

The view's kwargs are filled from the call's arguments before the class-level check. A permission scoping by a route capture reads view.kwargs["project_pk"] in has_permission, and off HTTP there is no URLconf to put it there; asked against an empty mapping it would refuse every caller it means to admit. Each method opts in to the kernel's arguments channel by declaring the keyword, and the names that go onto view.kwargs are the ones a route would have captured: route_reads, the arguments the spec's row lookup reads (pk of an update's instance lookup, or of a retrieve). Where a transport asks with no arguments at all (None), nothing is filled, and the classes decide what an empty route means, as they would for a URL that captured nothing.

The request and view the call carries come first. The class-level and object-level methods declare request and view, so a call registering either as a seed hands it over, and call_context, so a call that puts either in its context does: a transport running the kernel's dispatch carries the request a run arrived on, or a role view built for the operation, that way. Each is the seed, else the context's entry, and None in either place is no value. A carried view, or DRF Request, is asked as it is, with nothing filled onto it. Where the call carries one and not the other, the missing half is the offline pair's, built as below, so no class is ever handed None for a request or a view; where it carries neither, the whole offline pair is asked. The offline view's action is the call's context's action, where that is a non-empty string, so a class branching on view.action reads the operation's name; a carried view keeps its own. A carried Django request that DRF has not wrapped, the request a run arrived on as the kernel's call context holds it, is asked as a DRF Request around a copy of it, built as the offline pair is: its user the principal and its query string empty, replacing its own, which is the endpoint's the run arrived on. Asked with no arguments at all, nothing is routed and its own query string stays.

has_object_permission asks only about a model instance; any other target is allowed here, because a DRF class written for a row reads attributes off it.

has_scope_permission allows. The kernel asks it of a bulk call's set, a collection's rows and a create's None, and DRF has no such question: on HTTP, a create and a collection action run the class-level check and no object check, and a DRF has_object_permission handed a QuerySet or None would raise AttributeError or decide on the wrong object. The class-level check has already run, with the view's kwargs filled, by the time the kernel asks this one.

No state is kept between questions: the compiled spec holding this check is shared by every call and every thread, so each question builds its own request and view.

docs.title: Refusals that are DRF's as well
docs.text: Each class is the kernel's refusal and DRF's exception at once, so a caller of the kernel's dispatch catches it by the kernel's class and DRF's exception handler answers it with DRF's status.

docs.title: DRFInvalidArguments
docs.text:
Bases: InvalidArguments, ValidationError

The arguments were refused, as both the kernel's InvalidArguments and DRF's ValidationError.

Every published consumer of this package catches DRF's ValidationError by name - an MCP server answering "invalid arguments", an agent tool asking the model to retry - and DRF's exception handler answers it 400. None of them catches the kernel's class, so what dispatch refuses leaves as this, and an except written against either side catches it.

Deliberately not a service validation error, which the kernel's class is not either: a business rule stated by a service about well-shaped input is a different refusal, and an MCP server answers the two differently.

detail is the kernel's tree - fields, nested objects, rows under their int index - with every message an ErrorDetail. A message that carries a code (the kernel's CodedMessage does) keeps it, and one that carries none takes code, "invalid" unless given.

DRF's __init__ runs on purpose. By the order of the bases the kernel's runs, and it leaves detail as plain strings: DRF's handler still answers 400 with a byte-identical body, but get_codes() raises, so a test asserting the body passes on the broken class. test_get_codes_keeps_the_kernels_code_and_defaults_the_rest and test_every_message_is_an_error_detail are what fail without it.

Every published consumer of this package catches DRF's PermissionDenied by name and ends the attempt on it, and DRF's exception handler answers it 403. None of them catches the kernel's class, so a denial dispatch makes leaves as this, and an except written against either side catches it.

Deliberately not a service error, which the kernel's class is not either: an agent reads a service refusal as something to route around and keeps trying, where a denial should end the attempt.

Both __init__s run by name, so neither depends on the order of the bases, which is a choice (the kernel's first, as the class is named) and no test can tell from the other. The kernel's sets message: test_the_default_is_the_kernels_message fails without it. DRF's sets detail with the code given, which the kernel's super() chain never passes: test_a_code_given_is_kept fails without it.

Bases: ServiceValidationError, ValidationError

What an author callable's DRF ValidationError leaves the kernel route as, through translate_drf_refusals: a service, a selector, a precondition, a provider or an extend_queryset refusing well-shaped input by a rule of its own. A transport reading the kernel's classes answers it as the service's refusal, and an except written against DRF's still catches it.
