docs.title: translate_dispatch_errors
docs.text:
translate_dispatch_errors() -> Generator[None]

Re-raise the kernel's DispatchErrors inside the block as this package's dual-base classes.

Every published consumer of this package catches DRF's ValidationError and PermissionDenied by name, and DRF's exception handler answers only those; the kernel's own refusals reach none of them, and a view serves one as a 500. So the DRF edge runs the kernel's dispatch inside this block:

  • the kernel's InvalidArguments leaves as DRFInvalidArguments, with the same tree and every message's code;
  • its DRFNotPermitted as DRFNotPermitted, and its DRFPrincipalUnavailable as DRFPrincipalUnavailable, each with the same message;
  • a subclass of any of the three leaves as that class's twin, with the subclass's message.

The new exception is raised from the kernel's, so the traceback keeps where dispatch refused. Each dual-base class is still the kernel's, so an except DispatchError around the block catches what leaves it as well.

Left exactly as raised:

  • anything that is not a DispatchError, a service's own refusals among them;
  • a DispatchError that is already a DRF exception, such as a dual-base class a validator raised itself, which both ladders already catch. An author callable's DRF PermissionDenied and NotAuthenticated reach here as such a class, translated by translate_drf_refusals as the compile hands the kernel the callable, and the DRF edge restores the author's exception itself (its ValidationError reaches here as a service's refusal, not a DispatchError);
  • a DispatchError with no twin here, which keeps the kernel's class rather than be given a DRF answer nobody declared.

Use it as a with block, around await too. Not as a decorator on an async def: that would wrap the creation of the coroutine, not its run.

docs.title: translate_drf_refusals
docs.text:
translate_drf_refusals() -> Generator[None]

Re-raise the DRF refusals raised inside the block as the kernel's classes, still DRF's.

The reverse of translate_dispatch_errors: an author writes a service, a selector, a precondition or a permission class against DRF and refuses with DRF's exceptions, which a transport over the kernel's dispatch reads as nothing it knows. So the compile runs each author callable it hands the kernel inside this block, and DRFPermissionCheck asks each permission class inside it:

  • ValidationError leaves as DRFServiceValidationError, with the same detail and codes;
  • PermissionDenied as DRFNotPermitted, with its message and code;
  • NotAuthenticated as DRFNotAuthenticated, which DRF still answers 401;
  • a subclass of any of the three as that class's twin, with the subclass's detail and status_code.

Each is still DRF's class, so an except written against DRF's still catches it, and DRF's handler answers it with the status the author's exception had. It is raised from the author's, which it carries under TRANSLATED_FROM too, so the DRF edge re-raises the exception itself and every route that answered DRF's exception answers it as before.

Left exactly as raised:

  • a refusal that is already the kernel's, the dual-base DRF classes and a twin translated by an inner block among them, which a kernel route already reads;
  • any other exception, DRF's NotFound, AuthenticationFailed and Throttled included, which have no kernel class to leave as.

Use it as a with block, around await too, for the reason translate_dispatch_errors gives.

docs.title: translating_drf_refusals
docs.text:
translating_drf_refusals(fn: None) -> None

translating_drf_refusals(fn: Callable[..., Any]) -> Callable[..., Any]

translating_drf_refusals(fn: Callable[..., Any] | None) -> Callable[..., Any] | None

fn, its DRF refusals leaving as the kernel's classes; None for no callable.

What the compile hands the kernel in place of each author callable that runs within a call: the service or selector, the preconditions, the kwargs and input_data providers and extend_queryset. fn is called as it was, inside translate_drf_refusals.

It keeps what a reader of the compiled spec takes from the callable: the name, qualname, module, annotations and signature, and, of a function or a method, the docstring and the attributes (a tool description is read off the docstring). An async def stays one, since the kernel awaits it by its kind (test_an_async_service_s_refusal_is_translated_too); the signature is fn's, which the kernel binds the call by; the annotations are fn's and __wrapped__ is fn, so a provider's return TypedDict is resolved in its own module and still names the keys it fills (tests/service_specs/test_translating_drf_refusals.py).

Identity is not kept: the compiled callable is a wrapper, so inspect.unwrap is what reaches the author's own. A functools.partial or a callable object gets neither docstring nor attributes, as its __doc__ is its class's and a reader that tells a function from an object by inspect.isfunction would otherwise be handed that class's words. fn itself is never stamped, as it is the author's own function.

docs.text:
register_drf_row_errors() -> None

Register DRF's ValidationError as a refusal the kernel re-roots under the row that raised it.

A nested write runs a row service per related row, and one written for DRF refuses its row with DRF's ValidationError, which the kernel cannot name, so it would otherwise escape the write naming no row. Registered, it is re-addressed as the kernel's own refusals are - a collection's row under its int index, a message about the row itself under non_field_errors - and rebuilt as DRF's ValidationError, with every message's code kept, so DRF still answers it 400.

Process-wide and for the life of the process, as the kernel's registry is. Running it again does nothing, because the reader is one module-level function; a second registration of the class with any other reader is refused by the kernel.

Not a home for this package's dual-base InvalidArguments: the kernel reads its own InvalidArguments before any registered class, so that one leaves a nested row as the kernel's class, and reaches DRF's ladders through translate_dispatch_errors.

docs.title: base_serializer_context
docs.text:
base_serializer_context(*, view: Any, request: Any) -> dict[str, Any]

Build the baseline serializer context a spec-driven render starts from.

Over HTTP every serializer DRF builds carries get_serializer_context — {"request", "format", "view"} — so serializers routinely read self.context["request"] unguarded (build_absolute_uri, request.user, a permission check in a SerializerMethodField). What a call layers on - the serializer_context a SerializerValidator or SerializerPresenter declares, and a view's get_input_serializer_context / get_output_serializer_context - is additive, not a replacement for that baseline, so off HTTP — where there is no DRF view to ask — the baseline has to be synthesized rather than skipped. Without it the same serializer that renders over HTTP raises KeyError: 'request' when the spec is dispatched from an MCP tool call, a Pydantic-AI toolset, or a management command.

Two sources, in order:

  • view.get_serializer_context() when the view has it — a real DRF view (the HTTP bulk path renders through the same helper). It is the view's own documented extension point and may already be overridden, so it wins.
  • Otherwise DRF's shape, synthesized from the view / request the caller passed: the synthetic pair from build_offline_context off HTTP, or None when the caller supplied neither. format is always None — content negotiation is an HTTP-only concern.

The keys are always present, mirroring HTTP: a serializer reading self.context["request"] off HTTP sees the synthetic request (and None only when the caller passed no request at all), never a KeyError. Absolute-URI fields additionally need real headers — pass the ambient http_request to build_offline_context when the transport has one, as the MCP server does.

A seat's own serializer_context is merged over this by serializer_context in service_specs/utils.py, so a provider keeps the final say on every key — including these three.

docs.title: build_offline_context
docs.text:
build_offline_context(
    user: Any,
    params: Mapping[str, Any] | list[Any] | None = None,
    *,
    http_request: HttpRequest | None = None,
    action: str | None = None,
    kwargs: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
    query_params: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
    host: str | None = None,
) -> OfflineContext

Build the OfflineContext for dispatching a spec outside an HTTP request.

A spec written for the HTTP transport may read a DRF request or view: a kwargs provider, a request-scoped FilterSet, a serializer reading its context, and the DRF permission check evaluating permission_classes. Off HTTP there is neither, so this synthesizes both; hand them to dispatch as call_context={"request": context.request, "view": context.view}, and the spec keeps working when driven from an agent toolset, a management command or a task runner.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default user Any

Set as request.user, so callables and permissions that read it behave as on HTTP. request.auth is None, set without running DRF's authenticators, so reading it never replaces this user: a scope check off DRF is the transport's to make.

required params Mapping[str, Any] | list[Any] | None

Seeds request.data, straight into DRF's parsed-data cache (a synthetic request has no stream to parse), for a callable that reads it. It is not what the spec validates: the kernel validates the arguments handed to dispatch and never reads request.data.

None http_request HttpRequest | None

An ambient Django request to wrap, so its headers / META are available (the MCP server passes its real one); otherwise an OfflineHttpRequest is created. Either way the method is forced to POST, because mutation callables often branch on it. The caller keeps ownership: a request passed here is never written to. What gets wrapped is a shallow copy, so the method / GET / user this function sets land on the copy alone, while META, the session, the upload handlers and any body already read stay shared — headers and session writes behave as they do on HTTP, and the live request keeps its own method, query string and user for the rest of its cycle. Pass the request you are serving; dispatching several specs from one request is safe, and neither leaks into the next.

None action str | None

The view action name, exposed on the OfflineServiceView.

None kwargs Mapping[str, Any] | None

The view's kwargs, the off-HTTP counterpart of a route's URL captures, read by any callable that declares view and reads view.kwargs. Never merged into the call's arguments: a value the spec validates is an argument to dispatch.

None query_params Mapping[str, Any] | None

Seeds the request's GET QueryDict, the source request.query_params reads — how read-shaping params that are not spec inputs reach the serializer offline: a serializer branching on query_params, and a request-scoped FilterSet reading self.request.query_params itself. Values are stringified as on HTTP; a list / tuple becomes a multi-valued param. Replaces a wrapped http_request's GET — on the copy that is wrapped, so the caller's own GET still reads its real query string afterwards.

None host str | None

The origin the synthesized request reports, so build_absolute_uri — which DRF's FileField / HyperlinkedIdentityField call whenever a request is in the serializer context — returns real absolute URLs off HTTP. Accepts "example.com", "example.com:8000", or a full origin whose scheme decides whether links are https. There is no default: unset, absolute-URI building degrades to the relative URL rather than raising (see OfflineHttpRequest). Ignored when http_request is supplied, whose own headers are authoritative, so a caller can pass both unconditionally.

docs.title: renderable_serializer_class
docs.text:
renderable_serializer_class(declared: None) -> None

renderable_serializer_class(declared: type) -> type[BaseSerializer[Any]]

renderable_serializer_class(declared: type | None) -> type[BaseSerializer[Any]] | None

The class a serializer or dataclass declaration renders through.

A bare dataclass type is wrapped in a DataclassSerializer — the payload the kernel's schema already describes for it, field by field — and anything else comes back exactly as declared, None included. Instantiating the declaration directly works for a serializer and fails for a dataclass, whose own __init__ is handed many= / context=; resolving it here first is what lets both shapes render.

Every render site in this package resolves through it: a spec's SerializerPresenter, which a view, viewset or action presents through and whose output() audience_projection_for_spec reads, so an agent is shaped by the markings of the class it is actually rendered with; the OpenAPI schema; and the browsable API's form serializer. A transport that instantiates a declaration itself calls this and instantiates what it returns:

serializer_class = renderable_serializer_class(declared)
payload = serializer_class(
    value, many=many, context=base_serializer_context(view=view, request=request)
).data

A dataclass gets one class for the life of the process, so repeated calls return the same object.

The pass-through is deliberate rather than a check. A BaseSerializer subclass is the ordinary case, and a declaration that is neither is refused where its schema is derived; refusing it here as well would break a caller that renders through a serializer-shaped factory without ever deriving one.

docs.title: Types
docs.text: The shapes this package owns: the view protocol and its hook chain, the DRF-typed authoring helpers, the offline request and view a caller off HTTP hands a serializer, and the serializer-field marking and schema registry the seats read.

docs.title: ServiceView
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Minimal structural shape of a view as exposed to a kwargs provider.

Per-spec kwargs providers (ServiceSpec.kwargs / SelectorSpec.kwargs) receive the calling view typed as ServiceView. The Protocol pins only the attributes a provider can rely on across both the standalone Service*View classes and the viewset mixins:

  • request — the current DRF Request.
  • kwargs — the URL kwargs dict resolved by the URLconf (e.g. {"pk": 7}). Empty dict on routes without captured groups.
  • action — the viewset action name ("create", "list", etc.) on viewsets; None on standalone single-purpose views.

Keep the surface narrow on purpose: providers should translate view state into typed kwargs for the service, not reach for view internals.

docs.title: ViewHooks dataclass
docs.text:
The HTTP view's hook-chain contributions, resolved and passed down.

The kernel's dispatch is the single execution core, but the view layer owns a configuration surface the core knows nothing about: the get_service_kwargs / get_<action>_service_kwargs / get_input_data / get_<action>_input_data / get_*_serializer_context chains declared on MutationFlowMixin and its viewset mixins. Those are methods on a DRF view, so the core cannot resolve them; this carrier is how a caller that has resolved them hands them over.

These are the view layers only — never the spec's own providers. Each chain resolves view.get_<x> → view.get_<action>_<x> → spec.<x>, spec winning on overlap. The kernel owns that last layer, so a caller must leave the spec's provider out when resolving these; hand over the fully resolved chain instead and the core runs the spec provider twice, which a spec.kwargs doing a tenant lookup will not survive.

Every field defaults to None (contributes nothing), so a transport with no view — MCP, an agent toolset, a management command — simply omits the argument and the core behaves exactly as it did before this existed.

Attributes:

Name Type Description extra_kwargs Mapping[str, Any] | None

Merges into the dispatched callable's pool, beneath spec.kwargs.

input_data Mapping[str, Any] | None

Merges onto the client payload before validation, beneath spec.input_data; server-provided keys win over the client's.

input_serializer_context Mapping[str, Any] | None

Layers onto the baseline serializer context (base_serializer_context), beneath the Validator's own serializer_context.

output_serializer_context Callable[[Any], Mapping[str, Any]] | None

Lazy — a callable taking the final post-selector result and returning the context — because the output context provider is documented to see the exact instance being serialized, which does not exist until after the service and output selector have run.

progress Any | None

The view's own progress sink, resolved for both chains — a selector can be long too (a large export is a selector). Reach for it only when a buffered request genuinely needs it: if a request runs long enough to want progress, a task plus polling is usually the right shape, and this seam is for the cases where that does not apply (a streaming response, or a websocket sidecar the host already runs).

docs.title: OfflineContext dataclass
docs.text:
The HTTP-surrogate a spec needs when dispatched off the HTTP path.

Produced by build_offline_context. Its request / view feed the optional request= / view= arguments of dispatch, and the whole value is consumed by the kernel's permission check.

  • user — the acting principal (request.user is set to the same value); Any because the user model is project-defined.
  • request — the synthetic DRF Request (.user set, .data carrying the params), forwarded to spec callables that declare request.
  • view — the OfflineServiceView forwarded to callables that declare view and used as the view argument of permission checks.

docs.title: OfflineHttpRequest
docs.text:
Bases: HttpRequest

An HttpRequest with no ambient host, made safe to use.

Built by build_offline_context when the caller has no real request to wrap (a Pydantic-AI toolset, a management command, a task runner). A bare HttpRequest has an empty META, and Django resolves the host from HTTP_HOST / SERVER_NAME — so get_host() raises KeyError: 'SERVER_NAME' and takes build_absolute_uri() down with it. That reaches serializers through the most ordinary field there is: DRF's FileField.to_representation calls request.build_absolute_uri(value.url) whenever a request is in the context.

Two behaviours, decided by whether the caller configured a host (build_offline_context(host=…), which seeds META — a configured request is an ordinary one and none of this applies):

  • Host configured — nothing here intervenes. Absolute URIs are built by Django exactly as on HTTP.
  • No host — build_absolute_uri returns the location unchanged, i.e. the relative URL. There is no honest absolute URL to return: the process has no idea what origin serves it, and a guess (the first ALLOWED_HOSTS entry, say) would emit confidently-wrong links that look valid. A relative URL is the same thing DRF's own file / hyperlinked fields fall back to when there is no request in the context at all, so this is the shape those serializers already handle.

get_host() still raises without a host — but with a message naming the fix, rather than a bare KeyError from Django's internals.

docs.title: offline_host class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
offline_host: str | None = None

The configured host ("example.com" / "example.com:8000"), or None when the caller didn't configure one. Set by build_offline_context; when it is set, META carries the matching keys and Django's own machinery is in charge, so nothing on this class changes behaviour.

docs.title: build_absolute_uri
docs.text:
build_absolute_uri(location: str | None = None) -> str

Absolute URI when a host is configured; the location itself when not.

Degrading beats raising: the caller is a serializer field rendering a link, and a relative URL is a usable answer that its consumer can resolve against whatever origin it reached the data through.

docs.title: get_host
docs.text:
get_host() -> str

The configured host verbatim; a pointed error when there is none.

Deliberately not validated against ALLOWED_HOSTS. That setting rejects spoofed Host headers from untrusted clients; this value came from the project's own code, and there is no client. Requiring it to appear in ALLOWED_HOSTS would break the ordinary case of a worker or management command that renders links for a site it does not itself serve — and would add nothing, since a caller who can pass a host can equally pass one that is on the list.

docs.title: OfflineServiceView dataclass
docs.text:
A concrete ServiceView for dispatching a spec outside an HTTP request.

Spec kwargs / extend_queryset / context providers are typed against ServiceView — the structural request / kwargs / action surface. When a spec is dispatched off the HTTP path (a Pydantic-AI toolset, the MCP server, a management command) there is no DRF view, so this frozen value stands in:

  • request — the synthetic DRF Request built by build_offline_context.
  • action — an optional label identifying the operation; None when the caller has no meaningful action name.
  • kwargs — the URL-kwargs equivalent (e.g. parent ids), empty by default.

docs.title: MARKING module-attribute
docs.text:
MARKING: Final = 'drf_marking'

Key under which an :class:FieldMarking is declared in a DRF field's style.

Namespaced rather than bare ("agent") because style is a shared bag any library may write to. The namespacing is courtesy, not correctness: readers match on the value being an FieldMarking, so a marking under another key still takes effect and another library's data under MARKING is refused loudly rather than silently misread.

docs.title: JsonSchemaRegistry dataclass
docs.text:
Consumer-extensible type → JSON Schema fragment rules for the DRF seats.

Rules are tried in order and the first match wins, before the built-in mappings — so a rule both adds support for a custom type and can override a built-in. The matched fragment is copied per use, so callers may freely mutate the returned schema.

Immutable: extend returns a new registry rather than mutating, so there is no shared global state to leak across callers or tests. Start from DEFAULT_JSON_SCHEMA_REGISTRY, the empty base, layer rules on, and hand the result to a seat as its json_schema_registry=:

registry = DEFAULT_JSON_SCHEMA_REGISTRY.extend(
    fields=[(MoneyField, {"type": "string", "format": "money"})],
)
validator = SerializerValidator(MySerializer, json_schema_registry=registry)

That rule describes every MoneyField of the serializer as the kernel spec it serves compiles, where only what the kernel can state is kept: the field is a string there and format: "money", which is none of the kernel's four formats, is dropped (test_registry_through_the_compiled_spec's test_the_kernel_s_schema_states_the_rule_but_for_the_dropped_format). A rule extend prepends wins over the registry's own (test_a_rule_an_extension_prepends_wins_over_the_registrys_own).

Attributes:

Name Type Description fields tuple[_Rule, ...]

DRF Field subclasses, matched by isinstance when a SerializerValidator or SerializerPresenter walks its serializer.

Return a new registry with the given rules prepended (they win first).

docs.text: Each view takes a kernel spec on spec. See Concepts for what the edge reads from the request and how a refusal is answered.

docs.text:
Bases: MutationFlowMixin, GenericAPIView

POST endpoint that runs a service callable to create a resource.

Configure by setting spec to a kernel ServiceSpec. The view's success_status defaults to 201 Created when unset.

docs.title: ServiceUpdateView
docs.text:
Bases: MutationFlowMixin, GenericAPIView

PUT / PATCH endpoint that runs a service callable.

The instance to update is resolved via spec.instance_selector_spec — no queryset / lookup_field required on the subclass. A spec never falls back to DRF's get_object(), its target being its own lookup's, so as_view() refuses one that declares neither a target selector nor many.

Configure by setting spec to a kernel ServiceSpec. The view's success_status defaults to 200 OK when unset. Both verbs share the one spec, so a forced spec.partial applies to PUT and PATCH — set http_method_names = ["patch"] for a PATCH-only endpoint.

docs.title: ServiceDeleteView
docs.text:
Bases: MutationFlowMixin, GenericAPIView

DELETE endpoint that runs a service callable.

The instance to delete is resolved via spec.instance_selector_spec — no queryset / lookup_field required on the subclass. A spec never falls back to DRF's get_object(), its target being its own lookup's, so as_view() refuses one that declares neither a target selector nor many.

Configure by setting spec to a kernel ServiceSpec. Its validator is optional (for delete-with-payload patterns such as a deletion reason); the view's success_status defaults to 204 No Content; set output_selector_spec with a presenter on the spec to render a body instead.

docs.title: SelectorListView
docs.text:
Bases: ListModelMixin, GenericAPIView

GET endpoint that delegates to a selector spec or to get_queryset().

A kernel SelectorSpec on spec runs through the kernel's own dispatch and is presented by its own presenter, the page's rows alone when the view paginates, with the affordance answers it declares; a spec declaring neither presenter nor affordances is rendered by the view's serializer_class, as DRF renders a queryset.

spec = None (the default) keeps get_queryset() and the rest of the flow as vanilla DRF. The rest of the list flow (filter backends, pagination, response rendering) is the standard DRF ListModelMixin.

docs.title: SelectorRetrieveView
docs.text:
Bases: RetrieveModelMixin, GenericAPIView

GET endpoint that returns a single object.

A kernel SelectorSpec on spec runs through the kernel's own dispatch and is presented by its own presenter, with the affordance answers it declares. Its selector replaces get_object(): a miss is a 404, or, when the spec sets allow_none=True, a 200 with a JSON null body presented by nothing (the nullable-resource contract). A spec declaring neither presenter nor affordances is rendered by the view's serializer_class.

spec = None (the default) keeps get_object(), standard DRF lookup using queryset and lookup_field, as vanilla DRF.

docs.title: get_object
docs.text:
get_object() -> Any

Resolve the target row through the spec's selector, if one is set.

filter_backends do not apply here. DRF runs filter_queryset() inside its own get_object(), so overriding that method - this view, or any hand-written override - drops them. A tenant-scoping backend in DEFAULT_FILTER_BACKENDS scopes a sibling list view and not this lookup. Scope the selector's own queryset, or declare the rule as SelectorSpec.filter_set, which the dispatcher applies on both the list and the retrieve path.

docs.title: MutationFlowMixin
docs.text:
Bases: _ServesRaisedSchema

Provides _run_mutation for service-backed views and viewset mixins.

The flow itself lives in dispatch_mutation_for_spec, so @service_action can reach it without being a class; this mixin is the OO entry point that the per-action mixins (ServiceCreateMixin and friends) and the standalone single-purpose views compose, calling self._run_mutation(...) after resolving their per-action spec.

Four hook chains feed a mutation, each layered view-wide → per-action → per-spec and merged with dict.update so the more specific hook wins on overlapping keys:

  • extra service kwargs: get_service_kwargs → get_<action>_service_kwargs → the spec's kwargs provider.
  • the serializer's input dict, merged on top of request.data before validation: get_input_data → get_<action>_input_data → the spec's input_data provider.
  • the input serializer's context=: get_serializer_context (DRF's own) → get_input_serializer_context → get_<action>_input_serializer_context → the SerializerValidator's serializer_context.
  • the output serializer's context=: the same chain with output in place of input, applied during response rendering.

The per-action layer reads self.action, so it applies to viewsets only.

A kernel spec declares neither HTTP answer, so the response's two HTTP hooks are the view's: success_status and response_finalizer below, read off the class unbound.

docs.title: success_status class-attribute
docs.text:
success_status: int | Callable[..., int] | None = None

The success status: an int, or a callable declaring any of result / instance / request / view, or None for the action's default (201 create, 200 update, 204 delete). A body never goes out under 204, so a status resolving to it answers 200 with one; set, it applies to an answer with nothing to present too (test_callable_success_status).

docs.title: response_finalizer class-attribute
docs.text:
response_finalizer: Callable[..., Response | None] | None = None

The post-presentation hook on a 2xx: declares any of response / result / request / view / instance / data and returns a Response to replace the one built, or None to keep it (test_response_finalizer).

Resolve the mutation target, or defer to the core.

A spec's target is its own target selector's, or none: the view's get_object() is never asked for one, because the kernel takes a target only where the spec declares the selector that would find it, and refuses one handed to a spec declaring none. A standalone update or delete view refuses such a spec at as_view(); a caller that check never reaches (a viewset's action, @service_action) is handed no row (test_service_update_view's test_a_kernel_spec_with_no_target_selector_is_handed_no_row).

collection_selector_spec): there is no single instance. UNSET when

Any

with the right kwarg pool, error label and reserved-seed strip, and the

docs.text:
Bases: ServiceCreateMixin, ServiceUpdateMixin, ServiceDestroyMixin, SelectorListMixin, SelectorRetrieveMixin, ActionSerializerResolver, GenericViewSet

Router-compatible viewset wiring services and selectors.

Composes ServiceCreateMixin, ServiceUpdateMixin, ServiceDestroyMixin, SelectorListMixin, SelectorRetrieveMixin, and ActionSerializerResolver over GenericViewSet. See those classes for the configurable attributes.

docs.text:

Read-only viewset for list + retrieve.

Composes SelectorListMixin, SelectorRetrieveMixin, and ActionSerializerResolver over GenericViewSet.

docs.title: ServiceCreateMixin
docs.text:
Bases: MutationFlowMixin, _ActionSpecsMixin

Provides the create action; reads its config from action_specs.

Set action_specs["create"] to a ServiceSpec. When the "create" key is absent the action raises MethodNotAllowed. A non-ServiceSpec entry (e.g. a SelectorSpec) raises ImproperlyConfigured.

docs.title: ServiceUpdateMixin
docs.text:
Bases: MutationFlowMixin, _ActionSpecsMixin

Provides update (PUT) and partial_update (PATCH) actions.

The row is the spec's own target selector's, never get_object()'s. PUT reads its config from action_specs["update"]; PATCH reads action_specs["partial_update"] first and falls back to "update" — defining only "partial_update" yields a PATCH-only endpoint (PUT raises MethodNotAllowed). When neither key resolves, both actions raise MethodNotAllowed. A non-ServiceSpec entry raises ImproperlyConfigured.

docs.title: ServiceDestroyMixin
docs.text:
Bases: MutationFlowMixin, _ActionSpecsMixin

Provides the destroy action.

The row is the spec's own target selector's, never get_object()'s. Reads its config from action_specs["destroy"]; when that key is absent the action raises MethodNotAllowed. A non-ServiceSpec entry raises ImproperlyConfigured.

docs.title: SelectorListMixin
docs.text:
Bases: ListModelMixin, _ActionSpecsMixin

Compose with GenericViewSet.

An absent "list" key falls through to DRF's default get_queryset(). Any entry that is not a kernel SelectorSpec raises ImproperlyConfigured.

A kernel SelectorSpec under "list" runs through the kernel's own dispatch, as on SelectorListView: the view's filter backends and paginator apply to the set it read, and the spec's presenter renders the rows served, with the affordance answers it declares; a spec declaring neither is rendered by the view's serializer. get_queryset() still answers the spec's set to whatever else asks it.

docs.title: SelectorRetrieveMixin
docs.text:
Bases: RetrieveModelMixin, _ActionSpecsMixin

Compose with GenericViewSet.

An absent "retrieve" key falls through to DRF's default get_object(). Any entry that is not a kernel SelectorSpec raises ImproperlyConfigured.

A kernel SelectorSpec under "retrieve" runs through the kernel's own dispatch, as on SelectorRetrieveView: the view's object permission is asked of the row inside it, and the spec's presenter renders the row, or the view's serializer where the spec declares neither presenter nor affordances. A miss is a 404, or JSON null under allow_none. A kernel write spec never asks get_object(): its target is its own selector's.

docs.title: get_object
docs.text:
get_object() -> Any

Resolve the target row through the retrieve selector, if one is wired.

filter_backends do not apply here. DRF runs filter_queryset() inside its own get_object(), so taking that method over — as this mixin does, and as any hand-written get_object() override does — is what drops them. A tenant-scoping backend listed in DEFAULT_FILTER_BACKENDS therefore narrows the sibling list action and not this lookup, which is what makes the gap easy to miss. Scope the selector's own queryset, or declare the rule as SelectorSpec.filter_set — the sanctioned seam, applied by the dispatcher on both paths.

docs.title: ActionSerializerResolver
docs.text:
Bases: _ActionSpecsMixin

Resolve get_serializer_class() from action_specs.

A kernel ServiceSpec answers with its input serializer where the view sets no serializer_class. Every other case falls back to DRF's serializer_class, raising the usual AssertionError when none is set.

Example:

class InvoiceViewSet(ActionSerializerResolver, GenericViewSet):
    action_specs = {
        "create": ServiceSpec(service=create_invoice),
    }

docs.title: service_action
docs.text:
service_action(
    spec: ServiceSpec,
    *,
    detail: bool = False,
    methods: list[str] | None = None,
    url_path: str | None = None,
    url_name: str | None = None,
    **action_kwargs: Any,
) -> Callable[[Callable[..., Any]], Callable[..., Any]]

Wrap a viewset method as a service-backed custom action.

The decorated method's body is not executed — the decorator supplies the handler. The method exists so that @service_action can attach DRF @action metadata and pick up the action name from __name__.

Pass a ServiceSpec for the service wiring. detail, methods, url_path, url_name, and any extra **action_kwargs are forwarded to DRF's @action.

The spec runs through the kernel's own dispatch, as on the standalone mutation views: its permissions are asked there, after the view's own classes, a detail action's row is its own target selector's (never get_object()), and the answer is its presenter's, under the viewset's success_status (200 by default) and through its response_finalizer.

An AdditionalInputRequired answers 422 with its schema as raised on any viewset, DRF's own included. The restore runs inside the exception handler the view asks for, so the configured EXCEPTION_HANDLER runs once, and a handle_exception override on the viewset still has the last word on the body.

docs.title: selector_action
docs.text:
selector_action(
    spec: SelectorSpec,
    *,
    methods: list[str] | None = None,
    url_path: str | None = None,
    url_name: str | None = None,
    **action_kwargs: Any,
) -> Callable[[Callable[..., Any]], Callable[..., Any]]

Wrap a viewset method as a selector-backed custom action.

The decorated method's body is not executed — the decorator supplies the handler. The method exists so the decorator can attach DRF @action metadata and take the action name from __name__.

spec.kind drives both the dispatch shape and the DRF URL shape, so there is no separate detail= to keep in sync. SelectorKind.LIST is a collection action (detail=False) whose rows are a page where the view paginates; SelectorKind.RETRIEVE is a detail action (detail=True) whose row is null under allow_none and a 404 otherwise. For a URL shape that doesn't match the response shape, fall back to DRF's plain @action and write the dispatch yourself.

A SelectorSpec runs through the kernel's own dispatch, as on the standalone selector views: its permissions are asked there, after the view's own classes, and the view's object permission of the row a RETRIEVE finds. Its presenter renders the row or the page's rows, or the viewset's get_serializer where it declares neither presenter nor affordances.
